reviewBoundary: Six complete paired senior reading practices, two per grade. Fictional notices/narratives and qualified bird/tree/design/search explanations. Each has full three-question and four-question four-option passages. Same-author all-evidence/alternative review, no independent calibration.

units.title: A book swap and a delivery round
units.alignmentNote: Two complete original passages, three and four four-choice questions, following National I final structure. Old source supplies a level/family reference only.

materials.title: A book swap with a useful difference
materials.text:
The Elm Street Reading Room will hold a book swap on Saturday from 11:00 to 15:00. Visitors may bring up to five books and exchange them for the same number of available titles. Entry is free, and people who only want to browse are welcome, though browsing alone does not provide exchange tokens.

Books should be complete and in a condition suitable for another reader. Children's books, novels and general nonfiction are accepted. School workbooks with answers filled in, magazines and damaged books are outside this event's collection. Staff will check contributions at the entrance before issuing tokens.

Each accepted book earns one token, regardless of its original price or size. A token can be used for any book in the swap area. The event cannot guarantee that a particular author or title will be available. Visitors should not bring a valuable or personally important copy unless they are willing to let it go permanently.

A separate table holds books whose owners want to share a short recommendation. Writing a note is optional and does not earn additional tokens. Please keep private contact details out of any note that will be displayed.

Children under twelve must attend with an adult. Unused tokens cannot be exchanged for money, but may be kept for the next reading-room swap. Any books remaining at the end will be offered to the room's community shelves, according to the agreement made when they are accepted.

questions.prompt: Which item is within the accepted collection?
options: A workbook full of answers
A complete novel in good condition
A book with half its pages missing
A damaged magazine
questions.explanation: Complete usable novels are accepted. Filled workbooks/magazines/damaged copies are excluded.

questions.prompt: How are tokens awarded?
options: Five automatically for every browser
Only for a written recommendation
More for an expensive original price
One for each accepted book
questions.explanation: Accepted books earn one each, irrespective of price. Notes optional, browsers do not receive automatic tokens.

questions.prompt: What can an unused token do?
options: Require a valuable book to be returned
Be exchanged for cash at closing
Guarantee a particular future title
Be kept for the next swap
questions.explanation: Tokens may carry forward but not become cash or guarantee titles/return of relinquished books.

materials.title: The house after the corner
materials.text:
On Saturdays, I helped my uncle deliver groceries to several neighbours. I knew the streets well and was proud of finding every address without a map. Then Mrs Hart, who lived after the corner, asked us to use the side entrance instead of the front.

I assumed it was a temporary request. The front path looked clear, and the door was closer to the street. On the next visit, I carried the bag towards it automatically. My uncle called me back before I rang the bell. He had added the entrance preference to the delivery note.

Mrs Hart explained that the side door opened directly into the room where she could unpack the food. The front route required carrying everything along a narrow passage. From the pavement, I could see the shortest path to the building; I could not see the work that continued inside.

We asked the other regular customers whether their delivery arrangements still suited them. One wanted the bell rung only once because repeated ringing was difficult to hear clearly. Another preferred a particular time when someone would be present. We recorded agreed details without assuming every preference applied to every house.

The notes did not replace attention on the day. A closed gate or a changed instruction still required checking. Nor did they give us permission to enter anywhere simply because we had delivered before. They helped us ask a more informed question when something was different.

By the end of the month, I was less interested in proving I could find every front door. I wanted to complete the delivery in the way the recipient had agreed. My uncle still valued quick, accurate rounds, but accuracy now included more than a house number. Sometimes the most useful route began where the map's line appeared to end.

questions.prompt: Why does the narrator first head for the front door again?
options: The side-door request is assumed temporary
Mrs Hart has withdrawn her request
The uncle has forgotten the address
The side entrance has disappeared
questions.explanation: The narrator assumes a temporary preference and follows habit. Withdrawal/disappearance/forgotten address are not stated.

questions.prompt: Why is the side entrance more useful to Mrs Hart?
options: It lets the family leave groceries outside forever
It is always the closest point to the street
It avoids carrying food through a narrow passage
It prevents any visitor from ringing
questions.explanation: It opens into the unpacking room. The front is closer; storage forever/no bell are not the stated advantage.

questions.prompt: How are other customers’ requests handled?
options: Agreed details are recorded individually
Every house is entered without permission
All customers are told to change doors
One rule is applied to every house
questions.explanation: The narrative emphasises individual agreements, not universal rules or assumed access.

questions.prompt: What does accuracy mean to the narrator by the end?
options: Completing the agreed delivery beyond merely finding the number
Ignoring the recipient’s preferences to save time
Never needing to check a new instruction
Walking only the shortest visible route
questions.explanation: The ending extends accuracy to agreed recipient needs. Distance-only/no-change/ignored preferences contradict it.

units.title: A short performance and seasonal journeys
units.alignmentNote: Two complete original passages, three and four four-choice questions, following National I final structure. Old source supplies a level/family reference only.

materials.title: A place for a first performance
materials.text:
The Junction Arts Café invites new performers to a short open-mic evening on the first Thursday of next month. Spoken stories, poems and acoustic music are welcome. Each slot is a maximum of five minutes, including the introduction, so performers should plan within that limit.

Apply by sending a brief description and, if available, a short sample. A sample is helpful but not required. Places are limited, and an application is not confirmed until the organiser replies with a slot. Professional experience is not necessary; the evening is intended as a supportive first opportunity rather than a competition.

Performers must arrive at 18:00 for a brief sound check. The audience enters at 18:30 and the event begins at 19:00. A microphone and basic sound system are supplied. Bring any personal instrument or printed text you need. Recorded backing tracks are not used at this event.

There is no fee for performing. Audience tickets cost four pounds and should be booked separately; a performer's confirmation does not reserve seats for friends. The café serves drinks, but purchases are optional.

Tell the organiser in advance about access needs or a concern about the setup. If you can no longer attend, let the team know promptly so the time can be reassigned. The organiser may change the running order on the evening. A confirmed place guarantees a slot within the event, not a particular position in the programme.

questions.prompt: Which application can be considered?
options: Only one from a professional musician
One from a beginner without a sample
Only one requesting recorded backing tracks
One assuming an automatic slot without a reply
questions.explanation: No professional experience/sample is required. Confirmation needs reply and backing tracks are not used.

questions.prompt: When should a confirmed performer arrive?
options: At the end of the programme
questions.explanation: 18:00 is sound check.18:30 audience entry and19:00 start are later.

questions.prompt: What does performer confirmation provide?
options: Free seats for every friend
A guaranteed opening position
A compulsory café purchase
A slot, but no automatic audience seats for friends
questions.explanation: Slot confirmation is separate from friend tickets, running order and optional refreshments.

materials.title: The journeys we notice
materials.text:
The arrival or departure of familiar birds can make seasonal change visible. Yet migration is not one uniform journey repeated by every species. Routes, distances and timing differ, and even within a species not every individual necessarily follows exactly the same pattern.

A useful starting point is the resources a bird needs. Food availability and suitable conditions can change through the year. Moving between regions may allow birds to use places that meet different needs at different stages. This does not mean that every journey is easy or that movement guarantees a successful outcome.

Timing involves more than the weather on one morning. Seasonal signals and conditions along a route can influence when journeys occur. A local observer sees only one place within a much larger sequence. A bird that appears late at a garden may have faced conditions elsewhere that the observer did not witness.

The route itself can include stopping places. A wetland or coastal area may matter not because a bird stays there all year, but because it provides a place to rest or feed during a journey. Judging the importance of a site only by year-round residents can therefore overlook a different role.

Observation records become more useful when they preserve dates, locations and uncertainty of identification. A single sighting can be valuable, but an absence from one short visit is weak evidence that no birds used the area. Visibility, observer effort and the time of day all affect what is recorded.

These qualifications do not remove the pleasure of noticing a familiar arrival. They connect it with a broader process. The bird outside the window is both an individual in view and part of a pattern that extends beyond the garden. Asking which stage of a journey we are seeing can make a small local observation more informative without turning it into a complete account of the whole route.

questions.prompt: What does the opening caution against?
options: Treating every migration as the same pattern
Accepting that individuals exist
Recording bird arrivals
Recognising any seasonal change
questions.explanation: Uniform routes/timing are rejected, while observation/seasonal change remain valid.

questions.prompt: Why may a locally late arrival need a wider explanation?
options: Observers see the entire journey from one window
Only that morning’s garden weather can affect it
Conditions elsewhere on the route may have mattered
All birds follow one exact date
questions.explanation: A local view cannot reveal earlier route conditions. Fixed dates/local-only causes/full visibility are not supported.

questions.prompt: How can a stopping place be important?
options: Only permanent residents can use it
It supports birds during a journey even without year-round residence
It removes the need for food elsewhere
It guarantees that every bird survives
questions.explanation: Rest/feeding at a stage matters beyond residency. Guarantees/exclusive use/no later resources are not claimed.

questions.prompt: What improves the interpretation of local records?
options: Treating one brief absence as proof of no use
Assuming every observer sees the same things
Dates, locations and limits on what was observed
Removing uncertain identifications without noting them
questions.explanation: The passage values documented circumstances and uncertainty. Strong absence claims and identical-visibility assumptions are rejected.

units.title: Reviewing books and defining a design problem
units.alignmentNote: Two complete original passages, three and four four-choice questions, following National I final structure. Old source supplies a level/family reference only.

materials.title: Review readers wanted
materials.text:
The Westbridge Review is building a small pool of volunteer readers for nonfiction book proposals. Readers prepare private reports for the editorial team; these are not public reviews and must not be shared with authors or posted online without permission.

Applicants should submit a short statement of subject interests and a sample report of no more than 700 words on a published nonfiction book of their choice. The sample should explain an evaluation with reference to the book, rather than list approval or dislike. Applicants need not have a formal publishing job, but should demonstrate careful reading and reliable communication.

Selected readers may be offered occasional proposals that match their interests. An invitation can be declined if the reader lacks time or relevant knowledge. Joining the pool does not guarantee a fixed number of assignments, and no one is expected to accept every subject.

Before taking an assignment, disclose any connection that may affect impartiality, including a personal or professional relationship with the author. The editor will decide whether another reader is more appropriate. A report should identify its limits rather than pretend expertise the reader does not have.

Reports are normally due three weeks after acceptance. If circumstances change, contact the editor before the deadline. The purpose is to support an editorial decision with a reasoned assessment. A recommendation is one contribution to that decision, not a promise that the proposal will be accepted or rejected exactly as the reader advises.

questions.prompt: What should the application sample demonstrate?
options: A confidential proposal posted publicly
A reasoned evaluation supported by the book
A guarantee of future assignments
Only a list of likes and dislikes
questions.explanation: The sample must ground evaluation in the book. Lists/public confidential content/assignment guarantees are not requested.

questions.prompt: What should a reader do before accepting a connected author’s proposal?
options: Disclose the relevant relationship
Assume every relationship proves impartiality
Hide it to avoid delay
Send a public review directly to the author
questions.explanation: Connections are disclosed for editorial assessment. Concealment/direct sharing/automatic impartiality contradict guidance.

questions.prompt: How is a reader’s recommendation used?
options: As an automatic three-week extension
As proof the reader knows every subject
As one reasoned contribution to an editorial decision
As a binding publication promise
questions.explanation: The final paragraph limits its role. It neither guarantees outcome, universal expertise nor deadline change.

materials.title: Whose problem has been solved?
materials.text:
A design can be described as successful because it performs the task its maker defined. The more difficult question is whether that definition captures the problem experienced by the people who will use it. An efficient solution to a narrow task can leave a broader difficulty untouched.

Imagine a public information screen redesigned to display more notices at once. If success is measured only by the number of notices visible, smaller text may look like progress. A visitor trying to identify one relevant message from a distance may experience the same change as a loss. Both accounts can be accurate about the measures they use.

The disagreement is not necessarily resolved by adding still more information. The visitor may need clearer grouping, a readable size or a route to further detail. The design question changes when the user's purpose enters the account. The screen is then evaluated as part of finding information, rather than simply as a container holding text.

Users themselves are not a single fixed audience. Someone familiar with the building may know which abbreviation to seek, while a first-time visitor does not. A proposal that works smoothly for the designer can rely on background knowledge that an unfamiliar user has no reason to possess.

This is why observation and testing can matter before and after a change. Watching what people attempt, where they pause and what they misunderstand can reveal a gap between the intended task and the experienced one. Such observations still require interpretation; one confused visitor does not by itself describe every user's needs.

A careful account connects the proposed improvement with the people, task and setting for which it is claimed. It can name a benefit without presenting it as universal. Asking whose problem has been solved is not a demand for a design that satisfies everyone perfectly. It is a way to make the promise specific enough to examine, and to keep a neat internal measure from standing in for the whole experience.

questions.prompt: What is the main issue raised by the screen example?
options: More notices always make every screen better
A measure of more content may conflict with a visitor’s information task
All visitors have identical purposes
Small text is impossible to print
questions.explanation: Display capacity and finding one message can diverge. Universally better/physical impossibility/same purposes are not argued.

questions.prompt: Why might adding more information fail to solve the visitor’s problem?
options: Visitors never need any information
Organisation and readability may matter more than quantity
The screen has no physical size
Every notice must be removed
questions.explanation: Grouping/size/navigation answer the experienced task. No-information/no-size/remove-all claims are absent.

questions.prompt: What can familiar designers overlook?
options: That their design can ever be tested
The existence of any abbreviations
Every detail of their own building
Knowledge an unfamiliar user does not already have
questions.explanation: The passage identifies unstated background knowledge. It does not claim total designer ignorance or untestability.

questions.prompt: What does the author recommend?
options: Treat one internal number as the whole experience
Specify the user, task and setting behind an improvement claim
Require one design to satisfy everyone perfectly
Assume one confused visitor proves every need
questions.explanation: The conclusion calls for examinable specificity, rejecting universal perfection and simplistic single-measure/single-case claims.

units.title: Three short films and a useful drawing
units.alignmentNote: Two complete original passages, three and four four-choice questions, following National I final structure. Old source supplies a level/family reference only.

materials.title: Three short films at the youth club
materials.text:
The youth club will show three fictional short films on Friday evening. Doors open at 18:15, and the programme begins at 18:45. The whole event, including a short discussion after each film, finishes at 20:30. Booking is free but necessary because the room has limited seating.

The Red Door, twelve minutes, follows a child who receives a key from her grandmother without being told which door it opens. The search takes her through familiar streets and into a conversation she did not expect. It is a quiet story about a family connection, with no frightening scenes.

Rain on the Steps, eighteen minutes, has no spoken dialogue. Two neighbours repeatedly miss each other while sharing a staircase. Sounds, gestures and small changes in their daily routines carry the story. The film is particularly suitable for viewers interested in how pictures and sound can communicate without explanatory speech.

The Extra Ticket, fifteen minutes, is a comedy about three friends who think they have bought seats for the same event. Each has read a different part of the booking message. The confusion increases before they finally compare their tickets properly.

All films have English subtitles where relevant. The discussion is optional, but please remain quiet if you leave between screenings. Children under twelve must be accompanied by an adult. A booked place is held until 18:40; contact the club if you expect to arrive later. Snacks are sold separately and should not be taken onto the stage area.

questions.prompt: Which film uses no spoken dialogue?
options: The Red Door
Rain on the Steps
All three have no speech
The Extra Ticket
questions.explanation: Rain on the Steps explicitly has no spoken dialogue. The others are not described that way.

questions.prompt: What causes the confusion in The Extra Ticket?
options: The club removes every subtitle
Friends read different parts of the booking message
A grandmother loses a key
Two neighbours share no staircase
questions.explanation: The comedy centres on differing readings of booking information. Key/staircase belong to other films; subtitles are not removed.

questions.prompt: What should someone with a booking do if arriving after 18:40?
options: Contact the club about the late arrival
Enter the stage area with snacks
Assume the seat is held without limit
Demand that discussions become compulsory
questions.explanation: The held-until time requires contacting the club. Indefinite hold/stage snacks/compulsory discussion contradict rules.

materials.title: The bicycle on the workshop wall
materials.text:
On a visit to a bicycle workshop, I noticed a drawing in which every part of a wheel seemed to be floating separately. I thought it showed a broken wheel. The mechanic explained that it was an exploded view: a diagram separating parts so their positions and connections could be seen.

Nothing had actually exploded. The spaces were a way of making the arrangement visible. A small ring hidden inside the real wheel could now be noticed between two larger parts. The mechanic pointed to it on the diagram, then to the place where it sat in a demonstration model.

I asked whether the picture was enough to tell someone how to repair a bicycle. He said it answered one question well, but not every question. It could show which parts related to one another without explaining all the tools, adjustments and checks required for a real repair. A useful diagram was not automatically a complete set of working instructions.

A customer arrived carrying a wheel, and I watched the mechanic ask about the problem before touching it. He did not begin simply because the drawing was available. The actual condition of the bicycle mattered, and the diagram could not show what had happened to this customer's wheel.

Back at school, I looked again at a similar picture in a science book. I had used to admire its neatness without asking what its separated shapes meant. Now I could see both its value and its limit. It made a hidden relationship easier to inspect, while leaving some practical knowledge outside the frame.

For my project, I drew an exploded view of a simple paper model I had made myself. I labelled it as a diagram of parts, then added separate assembly notes. The two pages belonged together, but they did not need to pretend to be the same kind of explanation.

questions.prompt: Why are the wheel parts separated in the drawing?
options: To record an actual explosion
To prove the workshop has no real wheels
To show they have no relation
To reveal their arrangement and connections
questions.explanation: An exploded view separates parts visually for relationships. It is not a literal explosion or denial of connection.

questions.prompt: What does the mechanic say about using the diagram?
options: It is useful but not a complete repair procedure
It guarantees a repair without any checks
It shows the history of every customer’s wheel
It should be ignored because it is neat
questions.explanation: The diagram shows relations, not all practical steps or an individual wheel’s condition/history.

questions.prompt: Why does the mechanic ask the arriving customer questions?
options: Questions replace all tools in every repair
He has never seen a bicycle wheel before
The actual wheel’s condition is not supplied by the generic drawing
The customer must redraw every diagram
questions.explanation: The generic diagram does not contain the specific case. Ignorance, mandatory redrawing and tool replacement are unsupported.

questions.prompt: How does the narrator use the idea at school?
options: Claims the diagram alone teaches every skill
Copies a customer’s private repair history
Removes all labels from the model
Creates a parts diagram with separate assembly notes
questions.explanation: The project distinguishes complementary diagram and instructions. The other choices do not occur.

units.title: A tool library and a tree in town
units.alignmentNote: Two complete original passages, three and four four-choice questions, following National I final structure. Old source supplies a level/family reference only.

materials.title: Borrowing from the tool shelf
materials.text:
The community tool shelf lends hand tools for small household projects. Membership is open to residents aged eighteen and over. It is a lending service, not a repair workshop: volunteers can explain the loan rules and available information but cannot supervise a project at home.

A membership costs fifteen pounds a year. Most tools can be borrowed for seven days without a separate charge. Some larger kits require a refundable deposit, shown in the catalogue. The deposit is returned after the item is checked back in under the loan agreement.

Reserve an item through the catalogue before collecting it. A reservation request becomes confirmed only when the volunteer team replies. Popular items may already be on loan. Collect confirmed loans on Wednesday 18:00–20:00 or Saturday 10:00–12:00, and return them during those staffed sessions rather than leaving them outside the building.

Check the item with the volunteer before taking it away. Report a problem noticed later promptly and stop using an item if its condition is uncertain. Do not make an unfamiliar repair to a borrowed tool without discussing it with the team.

Renewal may be possible if nobody else has reserved the item, but it must be agreed before the original due date. Membership does not guarantee every tool is available at every time. The shelf aims to make occasional equipment easier to obtain while keeping its condition and movement clearly recorded.

questions.prompt: Who may join under the stated rule?
options: Only people already owning every tool
Only professional repair workers
A local resident aged eighteen
Any child without an adult
questions.explanation: Resident membership begins at18. Child/professional-only/full-ownership rules are not stated.

questions.prompt: When should a tool be returned?
options: Outside the locked building at any hour
Whenever a neighbour promises to notice it
Only after the membership year ends
During a staffed collection session
questions.explanation: Returns use Wednesday/Saturday staffed hours. Unattended or indefinite/neighbour substitution are not agreed.

questions.prompt: What is required for a renewal?
options: Ignoring any other reservation
Buying the borrowed tool
Agreement before the due date, if the item is not reserved
An automatic extra week for every member
questions.explanation: Renewal is conditional and agreed in advance, not automatic/purchase-based or overriding reservations.

materials.title: More than the outline of a tree
materials.text:
A tree in a town square is often noticed first as a shape: branches against a building, shade over a bench or leaves changing colour. Those visible features matter, but the tree's relationship with its setting extends beyond its outline.

Below the surface, roots need access to suitable soil, air and water. A narrow opening in a pavement may reveal little about the space available underground. Judging a planting place only by the size of the visible hole can therefore miss a major part of the question.

Above ground, shade changes through the day and across seasons. A bench under a summer canopy may receive a different amount of light after leaves fall. Calling it a shaded seat without reference to time can be useful as a rough description, but not as a complete account of every visit.

The surrounding surfaces also matter. Buildings can shelter or channel wind, while paving affects how water reaches the soil. The tree is not an isolated green object inserted into a background that remains unchanged by its presence. Its growth and the use of the square become linked over time.

Human activities add another layer. People may gather beneath it, tie notices nearby or walk repeatedly across the same patch of ground. Care has to consider those uses as well as the tree's needs. A plan that looks attractive on a drawing may work differently once the square is busy.

This does not make a casual observer responsible for diagnosing every problem. It offers better questions to ask of a proposal or description. What season does the image show? What space has been allowed below the pavement? How will people use the area? Looking beyond the outline turns a familiar feature into part of a changing place, one that needs to be understood through relationships rather than appearance alone.

questions.prompt: Why might the visible pavement opening be misleading?
options: It does not show all the underground growing space
It is always the exact size of the whole root system
It proves roots need no air
It tells every visitor the tree’s age
questions.explanation: The opening is a limited view of root conditions, not a full root map or age record.

questions.prompt: What makes the phrase shaded seat incomplete?
options: Light conditions change with time and season
Leaves remain identical throughout every year
A bench can never receive shade
Every visitor uses the square at the same hour
questions.explanation: The seasonal/daily variation qualifies the rough description. The other claims deny that variation.

questions.prompt: How does the author view people’s use of the square?
options: As proof a tree cannot exist in a town
As part of the setting that care should consider
As a reason every drawing is useless
As something unrelated to the tree
questions.explanation: Gathering/walking and care interact. The author does not ban urban trees or reject drawings entirely.

questions.prompt: What is the main recommendation?
options: Examine the tree’s relationships with its changing setting
Diagnose every problem without training
Judge a planting only by its outline
Assume an attractive drawing settles all practical questions
questions.explanation: The conclusion develops relational questions, not appearance-only or amateur diagnostic certainty.

units.title: A guide to names and a word not found
units.alignmentNote: Two complete original passages, three and four four-choice questions, following National I final structure. Old source supplies a level/family reference only.

materials.title: Using the Town Names Companion
materials.text:
The Town Names Companion is a reference guide to selected street, building and district names. It records documented forms and explanations, while distinguishing them from local stories whose origins remain uncertain. It is not a current navigation service, and historical entries should not be used as a substitute for up-to-date directions.

Main entries are arranged alphabetically by the name used in the guide's chosen reference period. A separate index lists earlier spellings and later names. If a familiar place does not appear where expected, check that index before assuming it has been omitted.

Each entry gives its source references and the dates to which they relate. A date attached to a document does not necessarily establish when a name first entered ordinary speech. Where the evidence supports only a range, the guide retains that range rather than assign a single year.

Map extracts are included to help identify the place discussed. They reproduce historical arrangements and may show routes or boundaries that no longer exist. Captions state the date and source of each extract; readers should preserve those details when quoting or reproducing a permitted image.

Corrections and new evidence can be sent to the editorial team through the form listed at the back. Explain the claim, identify the source and distinguish a personal recollection from a dated record. Suggestions are assessed before any revision is issued. A submission alone does not change the published entry, and the team cannot guarantee that every proposed explanation will be adopted.

questions.prompt: Where should a reader check an earlier spelling?
options: The café price list
The separate name index
Only the current navigation display
A randomly chosen map without its caption
questions.explanation: The separate index lists earlier spellings/later names. Current navigation/captionless map/café list do not supply this function.

questions.prompt: What does a document date not necessarily prove?
options: Which historical extract has a stated date
That the guide has source references
When a name first entered ordinary speech
Which document is being cited
questions.explanation: Earliest ordinary use may predate surviving dated documentation. Source dates do not settle that historical onset.

questions.prompt: How are submitted corrections handled?
options: Every personal memory replaces dated records
They are assessed before a revision is issued
They automatically rewrite the entry on submission
All suggested explanations are guaranteed adoption
questions.explanation: The team evaluates claims/sources before revision. Automatic change and guaranteed preference are explicitly denied.

materials.title: The word that did not appear
materials.text:
A student searched a collection of old newspapers for a word and found no examples. It was tempting to write that people of the period had never used it. The search had produced a real result, but the proposed conclusion went beyond what that result alone could establish.

The collection contained particular newspapers from particular places and dates. It did not include every conversation, letter or unpublished note. Even a perfectly accurate search of that collection would describe its contents, not all language used by everyone alive at the time.

The search method added another limit. A word might have appeared in an older spelling, or a scanned page might have been imperfectly recognised by the text-search system. These possibilities did not prove the word was present. They showed why a blank result needed to be understood in relation to the method.

Absence can still be informative. If a writer makes a specific claim that a phrase appeared in a named issue, examining that issue is directly relevant. A sufficiently complete record for a narrow question may offer stronger negative evidence than a partial collection used to answer an unlimited one.

The responsible response is therefore not to treat every failed search as meaningless. It is to state the scope: no examples were found in this collection, using these spellings and this method. Further searches may extend the evidence, while leaving room for the possibility that the word really was rare or absent from the material examined.

A careful sentence can preserve both the finding and its limit. The student's work becomes more useful when another reader can see what was checked and what remains outside the claim. Precision here does not mean replacing every conclusion with uncertainty. It means making the conclusion no larger than the search can support.

questions.prompt: What is the student’s initial overreach?
options: Noticing that newspapers have dates
Turning no results in one collection into a claim about all past use
Using a collection to investigate language
Reporting that a particular search returned nothing
questions.explanation: The leap is from bounded collection absence to universal language absence. The limited result/investigation itself is valid.

questions.prompt: Why mention older spellings and scan recognition?
options: To identify the word’s exact first speaker
To argue that no printed record can ever be searched
To show how the search method can affect a blank result
To prove that the word must occur somewhere in the collection
questions.explanation: Method limitations complicate interpretation without proving hidden presence or forbidding search.

questions.prompt: When may absence provide stronger evidence?
options: When the record is sufficiently complete for a specific narrow claim
When one newspaper is treated as every conversation
When the method and scope are left unnamed
When the collection covers only an unrelated place
questions.explanation: A named-issue claim is narrower and can match a complete relevant record. Unrelated/undefined/universal leaps are weaker.

questions.prompt: What conclusion does the author favour?
options: An automatic claim that every missing word existed
A rule that every failed search is worthless
A claim about all language from one unqualified blank result
A finding stated with its collection, method and scope
questions.explanation: The author preserves meaningful bounded findings, rejecting both worthlessness and unwarranted presence/absence claims.
